title: Combination Sum
description: Classic backtracking: explore every combination summing to target with unlimited reuse. A start index keeps combinations sorted and prevents duplicates like [2,3] vs [3,2].

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down what 'combination' and 'reuse' actually mean here.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given an array `candidates` of distinct positive integers and a `target` int, return every unique combination of candidates that sums exactly to target. Numbers can be reused unlimited times — so for candidates=[2,3] and target=7, [2,2,3] is valid (3 elements summing to 7)."

Quick clarifying questions:
• 'Unique combination' — order doesn't matter, right? So [2,2,3] and [3,2,2] are the same combo, return only one?
• Can candidates contain duplicates? (Combination Sum II differs — that one disallows reuse but allows duplicates in input.)
• Are all candidates positive? (Critical — negatives would make the search infinite because you could undo overshoots.)
• Could `target` be 0 or negative? (target=0 → just `[[]]`. Negative makes no sense for positive candidates.)
• Output order matters? Within each combo? Across the list?
sections.why: The 'positive candidates' question is load-bearing — if negatives are allowed, the recursion never terminates because you can keep adding-then-subtracting forever. The 'reuse allowed' framing distinguishes this from Combination Sum II (no reuse, but duplicate candidates), and 'order within combo doesn't matter' distinguishes from a permutation-style enumeration. Three sibling problems with three different invariants — naming them up front shows you've internalized the family.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious solution before reaching for the optimized recursion.
sections.say:
"The brute force I'd describe is: at each step, try every candidate (with reuse), subtract it from remaining target, recurse. Collect when remaining hits 0, abandon when remaining goes negative. The issue with this naive version is it produces every PERMUTATION of every combination — [2,2,3] would appear as [2,2,3], [2,3,2], [3,2,2], so I'd need a dedupe pass at the end. Probably sort each combo and stuff into a Set. That's correct but wastes huge amounts of work."

"The optimization is to enforce a canonical order during the search itself: at each recursion level, only consider candidates with index ≥ the current `start`. That way every combination comes out in non-decreasing index order — [2,2,3] is generated, [2,3,2] never is, no dedupe needed. Same recursion shape, one extra parameter, exponentially less work."
sections.why: Naming the 'dedupe after the fact' version explicitly is what makes the `start` parameter feel motivated rather than magical. Otherwise candidates write `start` because they remember the template but can't say WHY it's there. The framing 'enforce canonical order during search' is the load-bearing observation that transfers to Subsets, Combinations, and Subsets II — they all use the same trick for the same reason.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem says 'backtracking with target tracking'?
sections.say:
"This is a backtracking decision-tree problem with a twist: at each level, pick a candidate with index ≥ the current `start` (to avoid duplicate combos), and the recursive call passes the SAME `i` (not i+1) — that's what permits reusing the same number."

"The decision space at each level is: which candidate to pick from indices [start ... n-1]. Branching factor is up to n; depth is bounded by target/min(candidates). The two pruning rules: (a) if remaining hits 0, snapshot the path and return — that's the success base case. (b) If candidates[i] > remaining, skip (the value can't fit). If candidates were sorted, you could `break` instead of `continue` since all subsequent values would also be too big."

"Why backtracking over DP or iteration: this is enumeration, not optimization. DP would find the MINIMUM number of coins summing to target (Coin Change), or COUNT the number of combos summing to target — but if you need to LIST every actual combination, you have to enumerate them, and backtracking is the natural enumeration shape. The state is too rich for a DP table to recover: each cell would need to store every combination, which is the same data we'd build with backtracking anyway."
sections.why: The 'same i vs i+1' is the most diagnostic detail of this whole problem — i+1 gives you Combinations (no reuse), i gives you Combination Sum (with reuse). Naming it explicitly proves you understand WHY the code looks the way it does. The DP-vs-backtracking framing is the deeper insight: 'enumerate' is the keyword that disqualifies DP and forces you into backtracking. Coin Change vs Combination Sum is the textbook case-study — same input shape, different output type, completely different algorithm class.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to verify the recursion order and the reuse mechanic.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a couple of cases to confirm the start-index discipline and the same-i reuse mechanic." Three cases — a small case showing repeated 2s, an impossible target showing the empty result, and a larger candidate set showing all three branches.

examples.note: Standard case — [2,2,3] requires reuse (same i twice), [7] is a single-pick.
examples.trace:
backtrack(start=0, remaining=7, path=[])
  i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 5, [2])
    i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 3, [2,2])
      i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 1, [2,2,2])
        i=0..3: all candidates > 1 → continue
        return
      pop 2.
      i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 0, [2,2,3]) → BASE! res.push [2,2,3]
      pop 3.
      i=2 (6): 6>3 → continue. i=3 (7): 7>3 → continue.
    pop 2.
    i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 2, [2,3])
      i=1 (3): 3>2 → continue. i=2,3: too big → continue.
    pop 3.
    i=2 (6): 6>5. i=3 (7): 7>5.
  pop 2.
  i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 4, [3])
    i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 1, [3,3])
      i=1,2,3: all > 1 → continue
    pop 3.
    i=2 (6): 6>4. i=3 (7): 7>4.
  pop 3.
  i=2 (6): push 6, backtrack(2, 1, [6])
    i=2,3: too big → continue
  pop 6.
  i=3 (7): push 7, backtrack(3, 0, [7]) → BASE! res.push [7]
  pop 7.

examples.note: Impossible target — every recursion prunes or overshoots, res stays empty.
examples.trace:
backtrack(0, 8, [])
  i=0 (5): push 5, backtrack(0, 3, [5])
    i=0 (5): 5 > 3 → continue
    return
  pop 5.
(no other candidates)
res = []

examples.note: Three branches — pure 2s, mixed 2s+3s, and a 3-and-5 pair. Sanity-checks the same-i reuse on the 2s branch.
examples.trace:
backtrack(0, 8, [])
  i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 6, [2])
    i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 4, [2,2])
      i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 2, [2,2,2])
        i=0 (2): push 2, backtrack(0, 0, [2,2,2,2]) → BASE! push
        pop. i=1 (3): 3>0 wait — actually we never enter the loop body once we hit BASE because we return.
      pop 2.
      i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 1, [2,2,3])
        i=1 (3): 3>1. i=2 (5): 5>1.
      pop 3.
      i=2 (5): 5>4 → continue.
    pop 2.
    i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 3, [2,3])
      i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 0, [2,3,3]) → BASE! push
      pop 3.
      i=2 (5): 5>3.
    pop 3.
    i=2 (5): 5>6? no, push 5, backtrack(2, 1, [2,5])
      i=2: 5>1.
    pop 5.
  pop 2.
  i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 5, [3])
    i=1 (3): push 3, backtrack(1, 2, [3,3])
      i=1: 3>2. i=2: 5>2.
    pop 3.
    i=2 (5): push 5, backtrack(2, 0, [3,5]) → BASE! push
    pop 5.
  pop 3.
  i=2 (5): push 5, backtrack(2, 3, [5])
    i=2: 5>3.
  pop 5.

sections.why: Tracing the first example surfaces the single most-confused detail — why the recursive call is `backtrack(i, ...)` not `backtrack(i+1, ...)`. Watch how the [2,2,3] path goes i=0 → i=0 → i=1: it picks index 0 (value 2) twice before moving on. That repeated-i is the reuse mechanic in action. The impossible case defends the prune — every i either overshoots (continue) or recurses into a dead subtree. The third example's [2,2,2,2] branch is the most extreme reuse case and proves the recursion correctly terminates when remaining hits 0 exactly.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth calling out:"

• target=0 with non-empty candidates → returns `[[]]`. Base case fires before the loop, snapshot of empty path.
• Impossible target (e.g., candidates=[5], target=8) → returns `[]`. Every path either overshoots or runs out of valid candidates.
• `1` in candidates with reasonable target — recursion is fine but the result count explodes (target=10 with [1,2] → many many combos). Worth flagging that the runtime depends on target, not just on candidate count.
• Forgetting to pass `i` (passing `i+1` instead) → produces COMBINATIONS without reuse, not Combination Sum. Diagnostic: [2,2,3] never appears, only [7].
• Forgetting to loop from `start` (looping from 0 instead) → produces duplicates like [2,3] AND [3,2]. Diagnostic: result list is much longer than expected and contains permutations.
• Forgetting `[...path]` on the base case → all results alias the same array, when recursion unwinds they all become []. Same diagnostic as Subsets/Permutations.
• Non-positive candidates would make the search non-terminating — sanity-check this assumption in clarification.
• Sorting candidates first lets you `break` instead of `continue` on the prune check, modest speedup.
sections.why: The 'forgot to pass `i` and passed `i+1` instead' bug is the diagnostic-difference between this problem and its no-reuse sibling — it's the one detail an interviewer will probe ("what if I disallowed reuse, what changes?"). Knowing the answer is literally one character (i → i+1) is the proof you see the family. The non-positive-candidates note is the depth flex — it explains why the problem statement bothers to specify 'positive integers' in the first place.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(N^(T/M)) where N is the candidate count, T is the target, and M is the minimum candidate value. The intuition: branching factor up to N at each level, max depth bounded by T/M (you need at least T/M picks if every pick is the minimum). It's a loose upper bound — pruning collapses most branches in practice — but it's the right bound to state.

Space is O(T/M) for the recursion stack plus the path array. The output itself can also blow up — exponential in the worst case.

This exponential bound is inherent: the problem asks us to ENUMERATE all valid combinations, and the count of combinations can itself be exponential in target. Backtracking is doing the minimum necessary work for the asked-for output.

For extensions: same template handles Combination Sum II (candidates have duplicates, no reuse — sort + skip sibling duplicates + recurse with i+1), Combinations (k-of-n choose, no reuse, no target — recurse with i+1, base case is path.length===k), and Subsets if you drop the target entirely. Drop one parameter, change one line — whole family."
sections.why: Stating the exponential bound without apology is the move — enumeration problems CAN'T do better than exponential in the worst case because the output itself can be exponential. The 'Combination Sum vs Combination Sum II vs Combinations' triple is the textbook family — all three share the same recursive skeleton with surgically different choices on the `i` vs `i+1` and 'sort + skip dupes' axes. Naming the family proves you don't just know this problem, you know the genus.

walkthrough.intro: Step through combinationSum on a small candidate set. Each call has a `start` index (prevents [2,3]/[3,2] duplicates) and a `remaining` target. Watch: prune oversized candidates, push-recurse-pop, and notice recursion passes SAME i (not i+1) so the same number can repeat in a combo.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter combinationSum(candidates=${JSON.stringify(candidates)}, target=${target})`, state: { candidates, target } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init res=[], path=[]', state: { candidates, target, res: [], path: [] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `BASE (depth ${depth}): remaining=0 → res.push(${JSON.stringify(path)})`, state: { candidates, target, res: res.map(r => [...r]), path: [...path], start, remaining, depth } };
for (let i = start; i < candidates.length; i++) {

yield { line: 9, label: `PRUNE i=${i}: candidates[${i}]=${candidates[i]} > remaining=${remaining}`, state: { candidates, target, res: res.map(r => [...r]), path: [...path], start, i, remaining, depth } };

yield { line: 10, label: `CHOOSE i=${i}: path.push(${candidates[i]}) → ${JSON.stringify(path)}, remaining ${remaining}→${remaining - candidates[i]}`, state: { candidates, target, res: res.map(r => [...r]), path: [...path], start, i, remaining: remaining - candidates[i], depth } };
yield { line: 13, label: `UNCHOOSE i=${i}: path.pop() → ${JSON.stringify(path)} (backtrack)`, state: { candidates, target, res: res.map(r => [...r]), path: [...path], start, i, remaining, depth } };
yield { line: 17, label: `return res (${res.length} combination(s))`, state: { candidates, target, res: res.map(r => [...r]), returns: JSON.stringify(res) } };

reference.approach: Backtracking with reuse — recurse on i, subtract from remaining
notes: Recurse with the SAME i (not i+1) — that is what permits reusing the same number.
Loop from `start`, not from 0 — guarantees combinations are sorted and avoids [2,3] vs [3,2] duplicates.
Push a COPY (`[...path]`) on the base case. Saving the reference would store a snapshot that empties out.
Skipping candidates[i] > remaining is a small prune; sorting candidates first would let you break instead of continue.

options: Because `i+1` would skip past `candidates[i]` before the prune check fires, missing some valid combos
To allow the same number to be reused in the same combination
Because the for-loop already increments to `i+1` on the next iteration, so passing `i+1` would advance by two
Because `i+1` would shift the start index, producing the sibling problem Combinations rather than Combination Sum with reuse
questions.explain: `backtrack(i, remaining - candidates[i])` re-enters with the same floor, so the next level may pick `candidates[i]` again — that is what makes `[2,2,3]` reachable from `[2,3,6,7]`. The for-loop's own `i++` advances only the CURRENT level; it has no say in what the recursive call is allowed to see.

questions.q: Why does the loop start at `start` instead of 0?
options: Looping from 0 would re-enter the recursion with negative `remaining` and stack-overflow
It forces combinations to be in non-decreasing index order so [2,3] and [3,2] are not both produced
It skips candidates already added to `path`, preventing the same index from appearing twice in one combo
It avoids re-checking the `remaining === 0` base case on candidates the parent call already pruned
questions.explain: The floor makes every combination come out in non-decreasing index order, so `[3,2]` is unreachable by construction and no dedup pass is needed. It bans going BACKWARD, not staying put — reuse still works because the recursion passes `i`, not `i + 1`.

options: Spreading converts the typed-array view into a plain array so `JSON.stringify` formats it correctly
path is mutated by later backtracking — storing the reference would leave a hollow snapshot
`res` is a Set internally and rejects duplicate array references, so each push must be a distinct object
Without the spread, the path's prototype chain still points to the recursion's lexical scope and pins it in memory
questions.explain: `path` is a single array shared by every frame, and the `path.pop()` on the way back up would hollow out any reference already sitting in `res`. The spread copies the contents at the instant `remaining` hit 0.

questions.q: When does the recursion record a result?
options: When every candidate has been tried at least once at the current depth
questions.explain: `if (remaining === 0) { res.push([...path]); return; }` — the target is tracked by subtraction, so a combination is complete exactly when there is nothing left to pay. It can never overshoot into negatives because `if (candidates[i] > remaining) continue` refuses a candidate that is too big.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the backtracking template. The reuse-vs-no-reuse blank and the snapshot blank are the load-bearing ones.

blanks.hint: spread into a NEW array so later mutations do not corrupt the saved result
pass i (not i+1) to allow reusing the same index
shrink remaining by the picked candidate
undo the push before trying the next candidate

L3.prompt: Write `combinationSum(candidates, target)` returning all unique combos (numbers may be reused) that sum to target. Log `JSON.stringify(combinationSum([2, 3, 6, 7], 7))`.
hints: Pass `i` (not i+1) on the recursive call to allow reuse of the same number.
Save `[...path]` on the base case so later backtracking does not corrupt the saved result.
